claims.text: Pre-coating tungsten particles with a few-nanometer chromium layer before mixing and sintering will produce a coherent W–Cr–Cu interfacial region.
The Cr-derived interfacial region will reduce electron scattering at the W–Cu interface.
The Cr-derived interfacial region will reduce phonon mismatch or phonon scattering at the W–Cu interface.
Reducing interfacial electron and phonon scattering will increase the overall thermal conductivity of the W–Cu composite.
Chromium in the coating will react with adjacent copper during sintering to form a thin in-situ interfacial layer.
The in-situ interfacial layer will chemically bond the tungsten and copper phases.
The Cr-derived interfacial layer will lower thermal boundary resistance.
A nanometer-scale chromium coating will leave the bulk tungsten and copper phases chemically unmodified.
Leaving the bulk tungsten and copper phases chemically unmodified will maintain the composite's mechanical integrity.
Leaving the bulk tungsten and copper phases chemically unmodified will maintain irradiation resistance.
The chromium-pre-coated composite will have higher thermal conductivity than an otherwise comparable uncoated W–Cu composite.
The chromium-pre-coated composite will retain tensile and creep durability at least comparable to the uncoated baseline.
The chromium-pre-coated composite will retain irradiation resistance at least comparable to the uncoated baseline.
The proposed benefit is expected when the chromium coating remains only a few nanometers thick and is uniform.
Sintering at 900–1100°C under a reducing or inert atmosphere can produce the desired W–Cr–Cu interface if time, temperature, and pressure are tightly controlled.
Excessive interdiffusion or secondary-phase formation may negate the thermal-conductivity benefit.
Nonuniform coating or excessive interdiffusion may adversely affect mechanical properties.
